To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the divergence times of the endemic species of the Hawaiian archipelago can vary significantly depending on the calibration strategy used.
(1) divergence times are sensitive to calibration information, and (2) the age of island formation is not necessarily the best calibration point for divergence time studies.

(i) the age of island formation is not a reliable calibration point to date the diversification of island species; (ii) the age of the islands can be used to date the diversifications of island species if it is assumed that speciation occurs at the island formation; and (iii) the use of probabilistic calibrators can be used to evaluate this hypothesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the correct use of calibration information in the context of divergence time inference.
the correct use of calibration information in phylogenetic inference and the implications of this information for understanding the evolution of endemic species on islands.
the correct use of calibration information in molecular dating analyses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while the volcanic island age is a useful reference for dating the divergence time of endemic species, the age of the islands does not necessarily correspond to a speciation event.
the use of fixed calibrations is not a good practice, as it can yield misleading results, and the use of probabilistic calibrators is recommended.
, while some species may have diversified in association with the emergence of the islands, others have diversified after their formation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in order to infer divergence times, we should use the most appropriate type of information available for a given group of organisms.

1) the age of volcanic islands should not be used to calibrate molecular dating studies of endemic lineages, and 2) a more rigorous biogeographical approach should be adopted to test hypotheses about the timing of speciation events.
, in general, the use of calibration points in molecular dating should be done with caution, as it is a source of error that can lead to erroneous inferences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of calibration information should not be taken for granted and should be carefully considered when inferring divergence times.

, when using a calibration strategy based on island ages, it is important to consider the uncertainty in these dates and the potential for lineage divergence to occur before the island is fully colonised.
, by permitting the estimation of calibration uncertainties, the age of island formations may provide more robust estimates for divergence times.
